THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • Poverty: extreme poverty 5.3% (2022-23, World Bank USD 3.00 line); MPI 55.3% (2005-06) → 14.96% (2019-21) → 11.28% (2022-23, estimated); Tendulkar line 21.9% (2011-12) → 2.3% (2023-24).
  • Seven themes of measures: foundational dignity, human security, asset and connectivity support, livelihood mobility, financial inclusion and DBT, social security, targeted inclusion.
  • Critical analysis: decline is real but line-sensitive; churning poverty; job quality is the weakest link (94.11% of registered informal workers earn under ₹10,000 a month).
  • VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaces MGNREGA: 125 days, four focus areas, 60-day pause window, normative funding, weekly wages, admin cost 6% → 9%.
  • Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): JAM trinity, India Stack (UPI, PFMS, ONDC, GeM, DigiLocker, UMANG, CoWIN, and more) and DPI diplomacy.
Understand it firstA poor family has crossed the line only if it stays across it. Basic services (water, toilet, gas, power) lift dignity; insurance and food protect against shocks; jobs and credit let it climb; digital pipes (JAM + UPI) deliver all of this without leakage. Memory aid, not from the handout.

1 · POVERTY REDUCTION: FROM WELFARE DELIVERY TO CAPABILITY BUILDING
PYQ 2016 · 12.5m · PMJDY and financial inclusionPYQ 2022 · 10m · financial inclusion and growthHandout pp.121-125 (typed; figures on pp.121 and 124)
Understand it firstThe handout's point: poverty fell not only because of income support but because of basic services, social protection, financial inclusion, housing, health, sanitation and livelihood support together. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • India's poverty reduction story is not only about income support; it reflects a wider expansion of basic services, social protection, financial inclusion, housing, health, sanitation and livelihood support, which together improve the ability of poor households to move out of deprivation.
Data: progress on poverty reduction
  • Extreme poverty has declined sharply: as per the World Bank's revised poverty line (from USD 2.15 to USD 3.00 a day), India's extreme poverty rate stood at 5.3% in 2022-23, while lower-middle-income poverty stood at 23.9%.
  • Multidimensional poverty has reduced: India's MPI declined from 55.3% in 2005-06 to 14.96% in 2019-21, and further to an estimated 11.28% in 2022-23.
  • Recent decade saw faster poverty decline: multidimensional poverty declined from 29.17% in 2013-14 to 11.28% in 2022-23, lifting nearly 25 crore people out of multidimensional poverty.
  • Consumption poverty also declined: estimates based on the Tendulkar poverty line show poverty falling from 21.9% in 2011-12 to 4.7% in 2022-23 and further to 2.3% in 2023-24.
  • State-level convergence is visible: states with higher poverty incidence in 2015-16 have witnessed greater reduction in poverty, narrowing inter-state differences in multidimensional deprivation.

Critical analysis: poverty reduction and vulnerability
  • Poverty decline is real, but line-sensitive: Tendulkar-based estimates show 21.9% (2011-12) to 2.3% (2023-24). But the World Bank's updated lens shows extreme poverty at 5.3% and lower-middle-income poverty at 23.9% in 2022-23. → Extreme deprivation has reduced, but a much larger group remains economically fragile.
  • Vulnerable population above the poverty line: many households have crossed minimum thresholds but are not secure; a health shock, job loss, crop failure or debt burden can push them back. This is the problem of churning poverty. E.g., World Bank: extreme poverty 5.3% but lower-middle-income poverty 23.9% in 2022-23, so many people are close to economic insecurity.
  • Threshold-based metrics hide quality of life: poverty lines show whether people crossed a subsistence level, not whether they have stable income, savings, quality education, affordable healthcare and social protection. Similarly, MPI gains may show access to toilets, electricity, LPG or housing, but the quality and reliability of these services remain crucial.
  • Growth has reduced poverty, but mobility is uneven: growth has not always translated into broad-based upward mobility. A large informal workforce, low earnings and weak social security keep many households just above poverty.
  • Job quality remains the weakest link: poverty reduction becomes durable only when people move into stable, better-paid work. But e-Shram data shows 94.11% of registered informal workers earn less than ₹10,000 per month.
  • Rural vulnerability continues: the rural-urban poverty gap has narrowed, but rural distress has not disappeared. Dependence on agriculture, volatile farm incomes, small holdings and uneven non-farm opportunities expose many households to shocks.
  • Human development gaps constrain future mobility: poverty reduction must be linked with nutrition, learning and health outcomes. Poor learning outcomes, high out-of-pocket health costs, child malnutrition and weak service quality can reproduce deprivation across generations.
  • Inequality and exclusion need attention: poverty can fall even when gains are uneven across regions, classes, gender and social groups. Rising aspirations, graduate unemployment, low-paid female work and regional imbalances show that poverty reduction must be paired with inclusive opportunity creation. E.g., youth unemployment around 45%; unemployment among graduates close to 29%.

Way forward: from poverty reduction to economic security
  • Aim: not only to reduce the number of poor, but to ensure that households moving above poverty do not remain trapped in low-income vulnerability.
  • Track vulnerability, not just poverty: identify households just above the poverty line, most exposed to health shocks, job loss, crop failure and debt stress.
  • Build resilience against churning poverty: food security, health insurance, pension, accident cover and emergency support for poor and near-poor households.
  • Create productive and stable jobs: move people into better-paid, formal and productive work; growth must generate labour-absorbing opportunities in manufacturing, services and rural non-farm sectors.
  • Link welfare with livelihood mobility: complement housing, water, sanitation, LPG and electricity with credit, skills, market access and entrepreneurship support.
  • Strengthen rural income diversification: non-farm jobs, agro-processing, rural enterprises, SHG-led livelihoods and better market connectivity.
  • Use data for targeted intervention: frequent household surveys, local-level deprivation mapping and technology-enabled tracking to identify who is poor, who is vulnerable and what support they need.

2 · VIKSIT BHARAT GUARANTEE FOR ROZGAR AND AJEEVIKA MISSION (GRAMIN) · VB-G RAM G
Handout pp.125-126 (typed)
Understand it firstMGNREGA promised 100 days of work. The new Act promises 125 days, but with fixed work areas, a seasonal pause, fixed state-wise funds and heavy digital monitoring. Gains: more days and planning; worries: funds, demand-driven character, exclusion. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 is a comprehensive legislative reset that aims to modernise rural employment guarantees, strengthen accountability, and align employment creation with long-term infrastructure and climate resilience goals. It is a significant upgrade over MGNREGA, fixing structural weaknesses while enhancing employment, transparency, planning and accountability.
FeatureMGNREGSVB-G RAM G
Days of employmentProvided 100 days of wage employmentLegal guarantee of 125 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per financial year
Focus of worksMultiple and scattered categories, often with limited strategic focusPrioritises four clear areas: water security, rural infrastructure, livelihoods, and disaster / climate-resilience works
Unemployment allowancePayable if work not provided within the stipulated time, but disentitlement clauses existedPayable with clearer accountability; disentitlement clauses removed to strengthen the rights-based nature
Pause windowNo explicit statutory pause windowStates can notify up to 60 days during peak sowing and harvesting seasons when works will not be undertaken, ensuring farm labour availability
Funding approachDemand-based funding, but allocations could be unpredictableDemand-driven nature continues, with state-wise normative allocation based on objective development parameters for equity, fairness and balanced regional development
Local planningGram Panchayat planning was centralStrengthens decentralised, Gram Sabha-led Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans, integrating convergence and infrastructure planning
MNEMONICWater, Roads, Livelihood, DisasterWater security · Rural infrastructure · Livelihoods · Disaster / climate resilience: the four focus areas of VB-G RAM G works. (own memory aid)
Additional reform features
  • Timely wage payment: weekly, or at the latest within a fortnight of work completion.
  • Stronger administrative capacity: administrative expenditure ceiling raised from 6% to 9% of total expenditure (staffing, training, remuneration, technical capacity).
  • Localised planning with convergence: rooted in Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans, linked with systems like PM Gati Shakti; Gram Panchayats continue to implement at least half of the works by cost.
  • Assets linked with national priorities: assets added to the Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack.
  • Stronger monitoring and accountability: real-time monitoring, GPS-enabled tracking, MIS dashboards, weekly public disclosures, social audits at least every six months; biometric authentication and AI-enabled monitoring to detect irregularities early.
  • Corrective powers for serious irregularities: the Centre can investigate complaints, suspend fund releases and direct corrective measures.
  • Financial sustainability: normative funding, cost-sharing and disaster-linked support to make funding more predictable while reducing misuse and fiscal stress.
Challenges
  • Funding adequacy and fiscal burden: a legal guarantee of 125 days needs much higher, predictable funding; the 60:40 Centre-State sharing ratio for most states may strain poorer and high-migration states.
  • Risk to demand-driven character: normative allocation can improve targeting, but if it becomes a funding cap, the scheme may shift from a worker-demand based right to a budget-controlled programme.
  • Pause window concern: the 60-day pause may help farm labour availability but can reduce workers' bargaining power and limit public employment when rural wages are low.
  • Panchayat autonomy and local planning: if centrally defined priorities dominate, Gram Sabha-led planning may weaken.
  • Technology-linked exclusion: biometric authentication, digital attendance and Aadhaar-based payments may exclude workers due to connectivity gaps and authentication failure.
  • Wage adequacy and legal concerns: if wages are not linked to inflation, minimum wages and cost of living, the guarantee may not ensure dignity; a pending legal challenge raises concerns around federalism, livelihood rights and Panchayat autonomy.
Way forward
  • Back the guarantee with adequate funds: realistic allocation, timely fund release, special support for fiscally weaker states.
  • Protect the demand-driven nature: normative allocation should guide planning but not cap genuine demand.
  • Safeguard local democracy: final work selection must remain participatory, Gram Sabha-led and locally relevant.
  • Ensure fair and dignified wages: revise with updated inflation and minimum-wage benchmarks.
  • Create durable rural assets: water security, rural infrastructure, livelihoods and disaster preparedness.

3 · INDIA'S DIGITAL PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE (DPI)
PYQ 2023 · 10m · status, problems and improvements in digitalisationPYQ 2016 · 12.5m · PMJDY (JAM)Handout pp.127-129 (typed; figures on p.127)
Understand it firstDPI is a set of shared digital roads: identity (Aadhaar), money (Jan Dhan, UPI), data exchange (API Setu), services (DigiLocker, UMANG) and health (CoWIN). Anyone can build on them, so scale is huge and cost per use is low. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • The UN defines DPI as a set of foundational digital systems forming the backbone of modern societies, enabling seamless interactions between people, businesses and governments. India has moved from being a mere user of digital systems to a builder of population-scale digital architecture.
  • Key distinctions: the Indian model is characterised by scale, openness and integration; digital infrastructure acts as a "public good" rather than a closed, proprietary platform.
Foundations: the JAM Trinity
  • India's DPI emerged from a deliberate convergence of identity, banking and connectivity.
  • Aadhaar: biometric digital identity platform; over 144 crore numbers by March 2026.
  • Jan Dhan Yojana: launched in 2014 for financial inclusion; accounts grew to 57.71 crore with deposits of ₹2.94 lakh crore by March 2026.
  • Mobile phones and connectivity: around 85.5% of Indian households own a smartphone; 125.87 crore wireless subscribers; 5G in 99.9% of districts, so digital access is not confined to urban centres.
  • The rise of the DPI stack ("India Stack"): a national framework built on open APIs and public digital goods, evolving modularly across key sectors.

Examine the problems faced in this regard and suggest improvements.★ Write: Status: DPI stack figures (Aadhaar 144 crore, UPI 21.70 bn, 85.5% smartphones, 5G in 99.9% districts, DigiLocker, UMANG, CoWIN). Improvements: interoperability, open APIs, DPI diplomacy.Where / gap: Section 3. Gap: cyber-security and digital-divide problems are not in this handout.
India's DPI diplomacy
  • Driven by the ethos of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, India views technology as an inclusive global public good.
  • Strategic partnerships: MoUs with 24 countries (including Armenia, Kenya, Brazil) to share technical knowledge and architecture.
  • Cross-border UPI: live in 8 countries (e.g. UAE, Singapore, France), improving remittance efficiency and cross-border financial inclusion.
  • India Stack Global: a platform bridging India's experience with partner nations' needs, offering digital public goods as adaptable building blocks.
  • G20 Declaration and the Global DPI Repository: in the 2023 Presidency, India positioned DPI as a development accelerator for the Global South and contributed the most solutions to the Global DPI Repository.
  • CoWIN as an open digital public good: offered free as open-source software to assist global public health logistics.
  • MOSIP and sovereign digital identity: a modular, open-source framework for building national identity systems, explored by over 25 nations.
NoteConclusion (handout): India's DPI journey has matured into a comprehensive, interoperable architecture that underpins economic activity and institutional capacity. It proves that massive scale need not compromise trust, and that technological openness can coexist with strict regulation and security. India has become a premier global reference point for building resilient, democracy-enhancing digital foundations.

TRAPS AND EXAM-HALL RULES
TrapWhy it fools youExam-hall rule
Two poverty lines.Tendulkar: 21.9% (2011-12) to 2.3% (2023-24). World Bank USD 3.00: 5.3% (2022-23). MPI: 11.28%. Never mix them.Write the measure and the year every time.
MPI figure.11.28% (2022-23) is an estimate; 14.96% is 2019-21.Say "estimated".
VB-G RAM G days.125 days (not 100); pause window up to 60 days; admin ceiling 6% → 9%.Pair each number with its feature.
Normative funding is not a cap.The Act keeps the demand-driven nature but the handout warns normative allocation can become a cap.Present as a risk, not a fact.
GatiShakti project count.Ch7 p.119: 208 projects, ₹15.39 lakh crore. Ch8 p.129: 352 projects, ₹16.10 lakh crore.Quote with the source page.
UPI figure.January 2026: 21.70 billion transactions, ₹28.33 lakh crore.Always add the month.

  • Q1. VB-G RAM G guarantees: (a) 100 (b) 125 (c) 150 (d) 200 days
  • Q2. Maximum statutory pause window: (a) 30 (b) 45 (c) 60 (d) 90 days
  • Q3. Extreme poverty at USD 3.00 line in 2022-23: (a) 2.3% (b) 5.3% (c) 11.28% (d) 23.9%
  • Q4. Share of registered informal workers earning under ₹10,000/month: (a) 54.11% (b) 74.5% (c) 94.11% (d) 99%
  • Q5. Administrative cost ceiling under VB-G RAM G: (a) 4% to 6% (b) 6% to 9% (c) 9% to 12% (d) unchanged
  • Q6. Number of countries where UPI is live (handout): (a) 5 (b) 8 (c) 12 (d) 24

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

ABHA: Ayushman Bharat Health Account. digital health ID

AI: Artificial Intelligence. computer systems that do tasks needing human-like learning or judgement

AMRUT: Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation. urban water and sanitation

API: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient. the bulk drug that makes a medicine work

APY: Atal Pension Yojana. pension for unorganised workers

COVID: Coronavirus Disease 2019. the pandemic that hit GST collections and compensation

DBT: Direct Benefit Transfer. money sent straight to a beneficiary's bank account, cutting leakage

DDU-GKY: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana. rural-youth placement-linked skilling scheme, expanded in Odisha

DIKSHA: Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing. national school education platform

DPI: Digital Public Infrastructure. shared digital systems (ID, payments, data) that many services can build on

e-Shram: e-Shram portal. national database of unorganised workers

GIS: Geographic Information System. digital map layers used by Gati Shakti

GMV: Gross Merchandise Value. total order value

GPS: Global Positioning System. here only the name of Madhya Pradesh's Skill GPS career-guidance app

JAM: Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile. trinity used for direct benefit transfer

LPG: Liquefied Petroleum Gas. clean cooking fuel

MGNREGA: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act. 100-day wage employment law for rural households

MGNREGS: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. 100 days of wage work

MIS: Management Information System. dashboards for monitoring

MOSIP: Modular Open Source Identity Platform. open-source framework for national ID

MoU: Memorandum of Understanding. a written agreement between two parties (used in the Flexi-MoU skilling model)

MPI: Multidimensional Poverty Index. health, education, living standards deprivations

MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. small firms by investment and turnover limits

MSMEs: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. plural of MSME

NCD: Non-Communicable Diseases. lifestyle diseases such as diabetes

NPS: National Pension System. retirement savings scheme

NRLM: National Rural Livelihoods Mission. mission that promotes SHGs

OBC: Other Backward Classes. socially and educationally backward groups

OCR: Optical Character Recognition. text layer read from page images; can be garbled

ODF: Open Defecation Free. ODF Plus adds waste management

ONDC: Open Network for Digital Commerce. open e-commerce network that lowers commissions

ORS: Online Registration System. online hospital appointments

PDS: Public Distribution System. subsidised foodgrains through ration shops

PFMS: Public Financial Management System. tracks government funds to the last payee

PM: Prime Minister. head of the Union government

PMGKAY: Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana. free foodgrain scheme

PMGSY: Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. all-weather rural roads

PMJAY: Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana. ₹5 lakh health cover

PMJDY: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana. zero-balance bank account scheme for the unbanked

PMJJBY: Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana. life-insurance scheme; interns get cover under it

PMSBY: Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana. accident-insurance scheme; interns get cover under it

POSHAN: POSHAN 2.0. nutrition mission for children, adolescents and mothers

SC: Scheduled Castes. constitutionally listed castes with reservations

SHG: Self-Help Group. small group of women that saves and borrows together

SJY: Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana. Bihar livelihood scheme for the ultra-poor

ST: Scheduled Tribes. constitutionally listed tribes with reservations

UAE: United Arab Emirates. one of MSMEs' export markets

UMANG: Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance. single-window app for services

UN: United Nations. international body whose COICOP standard CPI follows

UPI: Unified Payments Interface. instant mobile payment system

USD: United States Dollar. currency used to state external figures

VB-G RAM G: Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin). rural employment law named in Chapter 8; not used in this chapter
